en: Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
The Chapter on the Village of Bhūta 13.
The Training Rule on Causing Resentment.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta was assigning lodgings for the Saṅgha and designating meals.
At that time, the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka were both junior and of little merit;
consequently, they received whatever lodgings were inferior and whatever meals were inferior from the Saṅgha.
Those monks complained about the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, saying, "Dabba Mallaputta assigns lodgings out of favoritism and designates meals out of favoritism.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant.
“How indeed can the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka cause the venerable Dabba Mallaputta to be censured by the monks?
… [and so on] … “Is it true, monks, that you are causing the venerable Dabba Mallaputta to be censured by the monks?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, cause the monks to revile Dabba Mallaputta?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And so, monks, you should recite this training rule:
"In the case of causing annoyance, there is an offense of expiation.
In this way, this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, thinking,
"The Blessed One has forbidden complaining; this far the monks will listen," began to criticize the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta in the presence of the other monks, saying,
"Dabba Mallaputta assigns lodgings out of favoritism, and he designates meals out of favoritism."
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... they complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the bhikkhus Mettiya and Bhūmajaka even grumble against the venerable Dabba Mallaputta? ... [The Buddha asked:
"Is it true, bhikkhus, that you grumbled against Dabba Mallaputta?"
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, disparage Dabba Mallaputta? …”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And so, monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘In censuring or disparaging, there is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).’”
"Causing to be censured" means:
desiring to speak dispraise of one who is fully ordained and has been appointed by the Saṅgha as the assigner of lodgings, or the distributor of meals, or the distributor of rice gruel,
or the distributor of fruits, or the distributor of hard foods, or the distributor of minor items.
If one, desiring to cause trouble or desiring to cause vexation, censures or reviles one who is fully ordained, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If it is a legitimate legal act and one perceives it as such, there is an offense of expiation for censuring or reviling.
If it is a legitimate legal act but one is uncertain of it, there is an offense of expiation for censuring or reviling.
If one perceives a legitimate act (*dhammakamma*) as an illegitimate act (*adhammakamma*), there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for censuring or complaining about it.
If one censures or complains about one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

[Likewise] if one censures or complains about one who is fully ordained, but who has not been appointed by the Saṅgha as an assigner of lodgings, an allocator of meals, or a distributor of rice-gruel.
If one, desiring to bring disrepute, desiring to bring ill-fame, or desiring to cause embarrassment, censures or reviles one who distributes fruit,
or one who distributes hard food, or one who distributes minor items— whether that person is fully ordained or not—
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

If one, desiring to bring disrepute upon, desiring to bring infamy upon, or desiring to cause embarrassment to an unordained person who has been appointed or not appointed by the Saṅgha as a distributor of lodgings,
a designator of meals, a distributor of rice-gruel, a distributor of fruits, a distributor of solid foods,
or a dispenser of minor items, censures that person— whether ordained or unordained— [this is an offense].
Or if she reviles him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is an illegal action and she perceives it as a legal action, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegal action and she is uncertain about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one perceives it as an illegitimate legal procedure, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if one complains or criticizes someone who is acting out of natural inclination, or out of favoritism, ill-will, delusion, or fear.
"In the case of one who is insane,
and in the case of the first offender.
The third training rule concerning censuring is finished.
